name: Expected Value Framework
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Why a String of Money-Losing Quantum Bets Can Still Be the Right Portfolio
lesson.summary: Expected value reframes a single negative-NPV quantum project as one draw from a portfolio of possible outcomes, showing how a small chance of an enormous payoff can make a whole strategy rational even when most individual bets fail.
lesson.body:
Expected value equals the sum, across every possible outcome, of that outcome's probability multiplied by its value. This tool resolves a tension left by the previous chapter: a risk-adjusted NPV judges a single project as though it were a near-certain bet, while expected value judges that same project as one draw from a probability distribution of outcomes, which is closer to how experienced venture investors actually reason about early-stage technology.

Here is a worked example. A deep-tech venture fund is deciding whether to invest $5,000,000 in a quantum computing startup. It models three outcomes: a 70 percent chance the company fails outright and the investment is worth $0; a 25 percent chance of a moderate success or acquisition, returning $15,000,000; and a 5 percent chance of a breakout outcome where the company's approach becomes a commercial standard, returning $500,000,000. Expected value equals (0.70 times $0) plus (0.25 times $15,000,000) plus (0.05 times $500,000,000), which is $0 plus $3,750,000 plus $25,000,000, totaling $28,750,000.

Against a $5,000,000 investment, an expected value of $28,750,000 implies an expected ROI of roughly 475 percent, which sounds absurd until you remember it is an average across a distribution whose single most likely outcome is losing the entire investment. This is the actual mathematical justification behind the venture funding frenzy discussed later in this book: a portfolio of twenty such bets, each individually more likely than not to fail, can carry a strongly positive blended expected value driven by just one or two breakout winners, the same model venture capital has used successfully for decades in software and biotech.

The catch, and it is a serious one, is that expected value is only as trustworthy as the probabilities fed into it, and nobody actually knows with confidence whether the true chance of a breakout quantum outcome is 5 percent or something far smaller. Cut that breakout probability by 90 percent, from 5 percent down to 0.5 percent, while shifting the freed probability entirely into the failure bucket, and expected value falls from $28,750,000 to $6,250,000. The expected ROI collapses correspondingly from 475 percent to just 25 percent, a return an ordinary index fund could plausibly match without taking on any of the technology risk. A single probability estimate, essentially a guess, is doing almost all of the work in deciding whether this is a great investment or merely a mediocre one.

This is the mathematically correct answer to the skeptic who says quantum computing investment is irrational because most of it will lose money. That is true and also beside the point, because rational portfolio construction under genuine uncertainty is supposed to include a large share of expected losers. The real question is never whether most individual bets fail, it is whether the blended, honestly estimated expected value clears the risk-adjusted bar, and that question turns entirely on how the probabilities were estimated in the first place, which is exactly what the next chapter examines.
